summary: Presents service provider requirements for MPLS traffic engineering that is aware of Differentiated Services. It aims to guide the definition and selection of a technical solution but does not specify one. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A road company wants to reserve space on its roads for different kinds of traffic, such as urgent and regular. This memo lists what it needs from such a system but does not build it.

questions: what is a class-type in mpls
subtitle: What service providers need if MPLS traffic engineering is to treat each Diff-Serv class of traffic on its own terms.

tldr.problem: Existing MPLS traffic engineering enforces a single bandwidth constraint shared by all classes of service, which cannot meet needs such as capping the share of voice traffic on a link.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out three provider scenarios, then lists requirements for Diff-Serv-aware TE (DS-TE): up to 8 Class-Types, per-Class-Type bandwidth constraints, preemption kept intact, and criteria for judging candidate solutions.
tldr.outcome: It specifies requirements only; the technical solution itself is out of scope. The memo was later updated by RFC 5462.

today: RFC 3564 is an Informational requirements document that has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: The Problem DS-TE Addresses
sections.content:
Some providers use Diff-Serv to offer several classes of service. Where they also want to optimize use of transmission resources, they can add MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE), but classic MPLS TE works on an aggregate basis across all classes.

For finer-grained optimization the memo proposes engineering traffic per class instead. Mapping the traffic of a given Diff-Serv class onto its own LSP lets it use resources on shortest and non-shortest paths and follow paths that meet constraints specific to that class. This is what the memo calls Diff-Serv-aware Traffic Engineering (DS-TE).

The target environments are networks where bandwidth is scarce (for example transcontinental networks), networks with significant delay-sensitive traffic, and networks where the proportion of traffic across classes is not uniform. The memo covers intra-domain operation only.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a road company counts all cars together. DS-TE lets it give ambulances, buses and ordinary cars each their own lane rules.

sections.title: Key Definitions and Traffic Mapping
sections.content:
The memo repeats Diff-Serv terms such as Behavior Aggregate, Per-Hop-Behavior (PHB), PHB Scheduling Class (PSC) and Per-Domain Behavior (PDB), plus the TE term Traffic Trunk: an aggregation of traffic flows of the same class placed inside a Label Switched Path (LSP). It loosely calls the set of traffic aggregates for one PSC a "class of service".

There are two ways to map a forwarding class's traffic onto LSPs. Either all classes share one Traffic Trunk and follow the same path (the current aggregate TE approach, which uses an E-LSP), or the traffic is split by class into multiple Traffic Trunks carried on separate LSPs that can take different paths. DS-TE takes the second route and computes a separate path for each LSP, taking into account each trunk's bandwidth requirement and preemption priority, plus class-specific limits such as capping a class at x% of link capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting every kind of traffic in one big truck, DS-TE puts each kind in its own truck. Each truck can then pick the best road for what it carries.

sections.title: Three Provider Scenarios
sections.content:
Scenario 1, limiting a class on a link. The memo gives the example that 10,000 uncompressed VoIP calls at 20ms packetization produce about 1Gbps of IP traffic, significant on an OC-48c network. For delay and jitter reasons an operator may not want more than a certain percentage of voice on any link, while other classes use the rest. Existing TE has only one bandwidth constraint common to all classes, so DS-TE must enforce different constraints for different classes.

Scenario 2, keeping proportions steady. With existing TE, the share of each class on a link varies with the order in which LSPs are set up, their preemption priority and failures, which makes it hard to configure scheduler queues. The example sets queue service rates to (45%,35%,20%) for classes 1, 2 and 3, and has DS-TE keep each class within its share even after a failure. Dynamically adjusting the scheduler from admitted LSP bandwidth is an optional extra requirement.

Scenario 3, guaranteed bandwidth. An operator selling a "guaranteed" service may need to keep guaranteed traffic below a given percentage of every link while still engineering other traffic under a looser constraint. Existing TE cannot express both.
sections.plainLanguage: A town wants to keep only so many fire trucks on one road, keep a fair share for each kind of vehicle even after a road closes, and promise some customers a reserved lane. One shared limit for all cars cannot do any of that.

sections.title: The Detailed Requirements
sections.content:
The DS-TE solution MUST raise no interoperability issues with existing deployed TE mechanisms, and MUST allow deployment at the needed granularity, for example only in part of the topology.

A Class-Type (CT) is the set of Traffic Trunks crossing a link that is governed by a specific set of bandwidth constraints. The solution MUST support up to 8 CTs and enforce a different set of bandwidth constraints for each. An implementation MUST support at least 2 CTs and MAY support up to 8, and administrators must not be forced to deploy all of them.

A Bandwidth Constraint Model defines the maximum number of constraints and which CTs each applies to. The memo illustrates the Maximum Allocation Model and a Russian Doll model, and requires the solution to specify at least one model and be able to support several, with up to 8 constraints.

Preemption keeps its existing semantics, regardless of Class-Type. A TE-Class is a pair of a Class-Type and a preemption priority allowed for it. With 8 preemption priorities and up to 8 CTs there could be up to 64 TE-Classes, but the practical requirement is support for up to 8, drawn from any subset of the 64 combinations. Administrators MUST be able to disable preemption.

The solution MUST also work over E-LSPs carrying a single class and over L-LSPs, MAY work over E-LSPs carrying several classes treated as one trunk, MUST allow different overbooking ratios per CT, and MUST NOT prevent standard priority mechanisms from being used for restoration.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book asks for up to eight kinds of traffic, each with its own allowance, and a way to decide who can bump whom when the road is full. It also says the new system must work alongside the old one.

sections.title: How to Judge a Solution
sections.content:
The memo does not choose a solution. It says solutions might extend existing TE protocol syntax (IGP, RSVP-TE) to carry multiple bandwidth constraints, or keep the syntax and change its semantics. It lists evaluation criteria that MUST be used: whether the solution satisfies every scenario and requirement, how flexible it is (number of Class-Types and PDBs per CT), how extendible, how it scales, and its backward compatibility and migration.

For bandwidth constraint models, work was in progress and at least six criteria were expected, including that the model addresses the scenarios, works well in normal and overload conditions, applies whether preemption is on or off, minimizes signaling load, makes efficient use of the network and minimizes implementation and deployment complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Before picking a design, the memo gives a report card: does it do the job, can it grow, will it stay fast, and can old equipment still work with it?

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The solution MUST address security aspects. The memo says DS-TE raises no specific additional security requirements beyond those of MPLS TE and Diff-Serv. The solution MUST ensure that the existing security mechanisms of both, including protection against DOS attacks, are not compromised by its protocol or procedure extensions, or else provide mechanisms to address this.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system must not open a window in a wall that was already locked. It has to keep every old lock working.
